newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Palm Oil - Southeast Asian prices seen in range.
newsitem.headline: Palm Oil - Southeast Asian prices seen in range.

text.p: Southeast Asian palm oil prices are expected to trade in a range this week as the market looks for direction, though the release of export data from a cargo surveyor could provide a lead, regional traders said.

"It's completely directionless," the general manager of a Singapore-based vegetable oil trading company said. "Demand is high, but production is also good. For every one factor, there's another to shoot it down."
Malaysian traders said prices were likely to move sideways until a clearer picture on the stock situation is seen.
Malaysia's palm oil stocks at end-September stood at 894,030 tonnes, up from 803,016 at end-August.

Benchmark third position January crude palm oil futures may trade in a range between 1,100 to 1,150 ringgit, traders said. The contract closed on Friday at 1,118 ringgit a tonne, against 1,121 a week earlier.
"Unless we get some definitive direction, we will probably drift in a fairly narrow range," a dealer said.
"It will struggle to get below 1,100. At 1,150, people are selling. It's very hard to get bearish with the export figures we have and hard to see a big move upwards. It's all pretty confusing."

Malaysia's palm oil export data for October 1-25, expected to be released by cargo surveyor Societe Generale de Surveillance (SGS) on Monday, could provide a lead, traders said. SGS put exports for October 1-20 at 514,229 tonnes.
"People will be looking at the SGS figures to see how demand looks," said a trader at a Western commodity house. "If the figures are along market expectations, we may have a quiet market."
Indonesian palm olein prices are expected to be steady in the wake of news that state-owned plantations are expected to see a sharp drop in production this year.
"The news is bullish and could help raise prices next week," one trader said. "But ample supply at the moment and weak prices in Malaysia could cap the upside."
An Agriculture Ministry official told Reuters on Friday that state-owned plantations were expected to see a 20-percent drop in output from the forecast 1.8 million tonnes this year.
He said the fall was due to weather, ageing trees and last year's shortage of fertilisers.

The official also said that state-run marketing agency KPB, which markets all the crude palm oil produced by state plantations, would resume signing export contracts for November after a freeze in October due to overselling. The news pressured Malaysian palm oil prices on Friday.
"A contraction in local supply coupled with the resumption of (KPB) exports should give the market a bullish tone (this) week," another trader said.
"There's also a feeling that the local market is oversold," he added. "Prices should be steady (this) week."
Palm olein ended last week at 1,345-50 rupiah/kg in Jakarta, down from 1,375-80 rupiah the previous week.
(with contributions from K.T. Arasu in Jakarta and Rene Pastor in Singapore.)
